items.title: App Server: expose target-scoped model-provider discovery without exporting credentials

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## What variant of Codex are you using?

App Server / clients embedding App Server, with custom model providers.

## What feature would you like to see?

Please expose a versioned, target-scoped model-provider discovery capability
that executes inside Codex's native provider owner and does not export provider
credentials to the client.

An App Server client can currently read config, global account state, provider
feature flags, and a model list. It cannot atomically establish that a discovered
catalog belongs to the same effective host/profile/thread provider connection
that will execute a turn. This matters for clients that support more than one
host, profile, project, or custom provider.

For custom providers with `requires_openai_auth = false`, the deprecated
`getAuthStatus` correctly returns no managed OpenAI token. A client also should
not reproduce Codex's native `env_key`, inline bearer, command auth, gateway
OAuth, keychain/login, or signed-request credential resolution.

### Preferred API: owner-executed discovery

Add a capability such as `modelProviderDiscovery` and a request such as:

```text
modelProvider/discovery/read
```

The request should identify a concrete native target, preferably a thread or an
owner-created draft. A cwd/profile target could be supported when it resolves
through the same config path used to start a thread.

The response should contain:

- the bounded model catalog or provider response;
- a versioned catalog format;
- an atomic, non-secret effective-target receipt;
- a clear `unsupported` result when the provider or target cannot support safe
  discovery.

The receipt should include opaque owner-issued revisions for:

- host, profile, and target binding;
- provider and effective config;
- endpoint and wire protocol;
- account binding, when applicable;
- credential binding, when applicable;
- owner process generation and a monotonic invalidation sequence.

These revisions must not be environment variable names, command strings,
keychain labels, credentials, or hashes of credentials.

The native owner should resolve authentication, issue the request, recheck the
receipt after the response, and return only bounded public catalog data. No
authorization header, token, cookie, signing key, command output, or reusable
authenticated client should cross the App Server boundary.

### Optional API: opaque request lease

Some providers use a model-catalog schema that Codex does not parse. For that
case, an optional one-operation lease could let a trusted Node-side client parse
the response without receiving credentials:

```text
modelProvider/requestLease/open
modelProvider/requestLease/execute
modelProvider/requestLease/close
```

The lease should be bound to the authenticated App Server connection, client
principal, target receipt, owner generation, registered operation, exact method,
exact origin, normalized path, request budget, and short expiry.

The caller must not be able to supply an arbitrary URL, headers, request body,
proxy, redirect policy, or credential. For a `listModels` operation, the owner
would execute a fixed `GET` and return only a size-limited body plus selected
safe response metadata.

This is an optional escape hatch. Owner-executed, owner-parsed discovery should
remain the preferred path.

### Required safety and lifecycle behavior

- Enforce exact origin, method, port, and normalized path. Reject userinfo,
  fragments, encoded path separators, dot segments, origin changes, and
  redirects.
- Apply the native network/proxy policy and a whole-operation deadline covering
  credential resolution, connection, decompression, and body read.
- Support cancellation and a post-decompression response-size limit.
- Recheck target/config/account/credential revisions before dispatch and after
  the response.
- Provide explicit receipt re-attestation before a client commits an asynchronous
  catalog result.
- Invalidate leases and receipts when config, provider, endpoint, protocol,
  account, credential, policy, target host, or owner process changes.
- Generate a new owner generation on restart. Previously persisted catalogs must
  not become active without fresh re-attestation.
- Keep secrets and secret-derived identifiers out of renderer IPC, errors,
  telemetry, logs, and client caches.
- Restrict lease operations to an authenticated privileged client. They should
  not be generally exposed to a renderer.

Suggested stable failure classes include:

- capability/provider/target/operation unsupported;
- target not found or not ready;
- stale receipt, owner restarted, lease expired or revoked;
- authentication unavailable or reauthentication required;
- policy or endpoint rejected;
- timeout, aborted, response too large, invalid response;
- rate limited or upstream unavailable;
- config changed during request.

Capability absence and structured `unsupported` must fail closed. Clients should
not fall back to reading Codex config files, process environment, keychain data,
auth files, or an unrelated global account token.

## Additional information

This builds on provider-owned mechanisms already present in public source at
[`89a7298a`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs):

- [`model-provider-info/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs/model-provider-info/src/lib.rs)
  defines effective provider routing and native credential sources.
- [`model-provider/src/auth.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs/model-provider/src/auth.rs)
  resolves provider authentication inside the native provider layer.
- [`model-provider/src/models_endpoint.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs/model-provider/src/models_endpoint.rs)
  already performs provider-owned model requests with authentication, timeout,
  response limits, redirect rejection for configured catalog URLs, and identity
  checks.
- [`models-manager/src/manager.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs/models-manager/src/manager.rs)
  rechecks provider/auth identity before publishing asynchronous results.
- [`app-server/src/request_processors/catalog_processor.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/catalog_processor.rs)
  exposes `model/list`, but its request has no target selector and its response
  has no effective connection receipt or lifecycle revisions.
- [`app-server/src/request_processors/account_processor.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/89a7298aff55db29f9cb2ad2430e3efe02b7a454/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/account_processor.rs)
  intentionally returns no token for providers that do not require OpenAI auth.

This request is related to, but distinct from:

- #29156, which concerns Desktop provider-aware model selection and history;
- #24286, which concerns parsing a specific provider's model-catalog response.

The requested capability is a lower-level App Server contract usable by multiple
trusted clients. It does not require a particular Desktop picker design or a
particular provider schema.

### Compatibility and migration

1. Advertise the feature and protocol major/minor version during initialization
   or through a capability-read method.
2. Keep existing `model/list` behavior for clients that do not negotiate the new
   capability.
3. Implement receipts and bounded discovery in `model-provider` and App Server,
   reusing the current auth, routing, HTTP policy, recovery, and models-manager
   paths.
4. Let native hosts expose only a privileged target handle and App Server client;
   keep credential resolution in Rust.
5. Enable automatic external-client discovery only after successful capability
   negotiation and target attestation. Do not infer support from a version string.

### Suggested tests

- Receipt stability and revision rotation for config, provider, endpoint,
  protocol, account, credential, policy, target, and owner restart.
- Env, inline bearer, command auth, gateway/keychain/login, and signed provider
  paths remain owner-resolved and never serialize credentials.
- Origin/path/port normalization, redirect rejection, DNS/private-address policy,
  timeout, cancellation, decompressed-size limit, and sanitized errors.
- Config/account/credential changes before dispatch, during response read, and
  before result publication.
- Lease expiry, replay from another connection, cross-window isolation, and
  renderer denial.
- Protocol schema compatibility, major-version mismatch, method absence, and
  structured unsupported behavior.
- App Server integration for thread, draft, and cwd/profile targets, including
  restart re-attestation and stale-cache rejection.

items.body:
## Problem

`codex plugin list --json` fetches installed-plugin state remotely even when the marketplace catalog is cached. Local tooling therefore cannot obtain this inventory independently of network latency.

My custom skill-budget hook intermittently fails because it gives discovery seven seconds within a ten-second `SessionStart` limit. Both limits are local configuration.

## Observed behavior

- macOS; app-bundled `codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2`; signed-in profile with local and remote plugins.
- Reproduced `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` after seven seconds. Later listings succeeded in 3.6–4.9 seconds without configuration changes.
- Catalog caches were about ten minutes old when inspected, within their three-hour freshness window.

On an existing profile with remote plugins, this reproduces the caller's deadline:

```python
import subprocess

subprocess.run(
    ["/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex",
     "plugin", "list", "--json"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=7, check=True,
)
```

The timeout is intermittent. These timings are individual observations; I have not isolated transport, service, or initialization delays, or tested deliberately offline.

## Source-level behavior

In the matching version, [`run_plugin_list`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.155.0-alpha.9.2/codex-rs/cli/src/plugin_cmd.rs#L244-L254) awaits remote discovery. That discovery [joins the cached catalog lookup with a live installed-plugin fetch](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.155.0-alpha.9.2/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/remote.rs#L1197-L1207). Remote requests have a [30-second timeout](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.155.0-alpha.9.2/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/remote.rs#L107), exceeding this hook's budget.

## Requested behavior

Add a cached/local-only inventory mode, or equivalent supported API, that:

- Returns local plugin metadata and available enablement state without network requests, including when offline.
- Uses last-known remote state with explicit freshness/completeness information.
- Reports missing or unreadable snapshots instead of treating them as an empty inventory.
- Preserves live listing for callers requiring fresh account state.

This would let startup hooks use clearly qualified local data without waiting for remote discovery.

## Related work

- [#42150](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/42150): remote marketplace support in the CLI.
- [#34849](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/34849): catalog caching; installed-state discovery remains live.
- [#40137](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/40137): related startup latency, involving different metadata requests.

items.title: Hook review flow grants trust to every pending hook in one approval, across plugins and events, with no per-hook choice

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: hooks
labels.description: Issues related to event hooks

items.body:
## Summary

The interactive hook review flow presents every pending hook as a single approval. A user
who runs it to trust one hook also grants trust to every other untrusted hook, including
hooks contributed by plugins and hooks on unrelated events. There is no per-hook choice.

On this machine, one approval took the trusted set from one hook to five, spanning three
different sources and four different events.

## Environment

- Codex CLI: `0.155.1` (standalone, terminal)
- Desktop app bundled CLI: `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`
- OS: Windows 11, 10.0.26100

## What happened

The goal was to trust a single `PreToolUse` guard hook declared in the user `config.toml`.
Before the review flow, `config.toml` contained exactly one `hooks.state` entry:

```
<config path>:pre_tool_use:0:0
```

The user reports a single prompt covering all pending hooks, approved once. Immediately
afterwards `config.toml` contained five entries:

```
<config path>:pre_tool_use:0:0          (already trusted)
<config path>:pre_tool_use:1:0          (the intended hook)
<plugin-a>@<plugin-a>:hooks/<file>.json:session_start:0:0
<plugin-a>@<plugin-a>:hooks/<file>.json:user_prompt_submit:0:0
<plugin-b>@<plugin-b>:hooks/hooks.json:session_end:0:0
```

Three of the four newly trusted hooks came from two plugins, not from the user's own
config, and they run on `session_start`, `user_prompt_submit` and `session_end`. A hook on
`user_prompt_submit` runs on every prompt from that point on.

## Why this matters

Hook trust is the control that stops an unreviewed command running automatically. Bundling
the decision weakens it in a specific way: the hook a user actively wants becomes the
reason they accept everything else pending. A plugin that registers hooks needs only to be
installed and waiting when the user next has a reason to open the review flow.

This compounds with #47283. The desktop app offers no way to grant hook trust, so a user
who wants one hook trusted is pushed to the terminal flow, which is all or nothing.

I am not claiming an exploit here, and the plugins in this case were the user's own. The
point is that the approval's scope is decided by what happens to be pending rather than by
the user.

## Expected

  comes from the person who ran it, not from my own use of the UI.

to trust with its source and event so the scope of one approval is visible before it is

items.body:
## Summary

In the Codex desktop app, the `/hooks` screen shows a registered but untrusted `PreToolUse`
hook as enabled, with no action to trust it. The hook is silently skipped, the screen gives
no indication that it is not running, and approving from that screen writes nothing to
`config.toml`. Running `codex` in a plain terminal presents a review flow for the same
hook, and approving there writes the `hooks.state` block immediately.

The trust gate itself is reasonable. The problem is that the desktop app presents a hook
that cannot run as though it is active, and the one interface that can grant trust is not
reachable from the app.

## Environment

- Desktop app bundled CLI: `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`
- Standalone CLI on PATH: `0.155.1`
- OS: Windows 11, 10.0.26100
- Both share the default `CODEX_HOME`, so both read and write the same
  `C:\Users\<user>\.codex\config.toml`

## Reproduction

1. Register two `PreToolUse` command hooks in `config.toml` as separate groups, each with
   matcher `^Bash$`, so they occupy `pre_tool_use:0:0` and `pre_tool_use:1:0`.
2. Arrange for position 0 to be trusted and position 1 to be untrusted. A
   `[hooks.state.'<config path>:pre_tool_use:0:0']` block with a `trusted_hash`, and no
   block for `1:0`.
3. Open the desktop app and view `/hooks`.
4. Approve the untrusted hook from that screen, then restart the app.
5. Read `config.toml`.
6. Now run `codex` in a plain terminal, approve the hook in the review flow it presents,
   and read `config.toml` again.

## Expected

Either the desktop app grants trust and writes the `hooks.state` block for `1:0`, or it
shows the hook as untrusted and not running, and says where trust can be granted.

## Actual

Steps 3 and 4 produce no `hooks.state` block for `1:0`. The user reports that `/hooks` lists
a single row for the hook, shows it as enabled, and offers no trust action. Repeating the
approval and restarting the app several times changed nothing in the file.

Step 6 writes the block immediately, and the hook then runs.

## Evidence

Timestamps and contents of the same `config.toml` across one evening:

| Time | `hooks.state` blocks present | Event |
|---|---|---|
| 10:17:14 PM | `pre_tool_use:0:0` only | before any attempt |
| 10:37:24 PM | `pre_tool_use:0:0` only | file rewritten on app start, after two approvals in the app |
| 11:05:31 PM | `0:0`, `1:0`, and three plugin hook keys | after one approval in the terminal TUI |

The app does rewrite `config.toml` on start, so the file is being written; the trust block
simply never appears. Before the terminal run, no file anywhere under `.codex`, including
eight config backups, contained a `pre_tool_use:1:0` key.

Two further gaps make this hard to diagnose:

- `codex doctor` reports no hook or trust state at all. On this machine, with a guard hook
  registered, enabled and skipped for trust, it reported `19 ok, 1 idle, 6 notes, 4 warn,
  0 fail`, and nothing about hooks.
- The CLI has no `hooks` subcommand, so there is no way to inspect or set trust outside the
  interactive flows.

Detecting the problem at all required an external script that parses `config.toml` for
`hooks.state` keys. Anyone relying on the app's own surfaces would conclude the hook was
running.

## Relationship to existing issues

- #46210 establishes from source that `trusted_hash` is written only by the interactive TUI
  review flow, and that no CLI or exec path writes it. This report is the desktop app case
  of that finding, with the added problem that the app shows the hook as enabled.
- #40247 reports trust not persisting on Windows, where `config.toml` gains a new timestamp
  after the trust action but no trust content. The file behaviour matches what is seen here,
  though in this case the terminal flow did persist correctly.

## What was and was not checked

Checked directly:

- `config.toml` contents and timestamps at each step above.
- Absence of any `pre_tool_use:1:0` key across `.codex` and its backups before the terminal
  run, and its presence after.
- `codex doctor` output, and the absence of a `hooks` subcommand in `codex --help`.

Not checked by me:

- The desktop app's `/hooks` screen itself. The description of what it displays and offers
  comes from the person operating the app, not from my own use of the UI.
- Whether the app has a trust flow elsewhere that was not found.
- Whether the same happens on macOS or Linux builds.

## Ask

Could the desktop app either grant hook trust directly, or show an untrusted hook as not
running and point to the terminal review flow? Failing that, could `codex doctor` report
enabled hooks that are being skipped for trust, so the gap is visible somewhere other than
by parsing `config.toml` by hand?

The bundled-approval behaviour originally noted here is now tracked separately in #47285.

Subscription: not included; not verified for this report.

### Summary
Local browser-driven validation previously worked through a loopback HTTP development URL. After moving the prototype into its project directory, the preview entry changed to a file URL and Browser Use rejected it. The rejection also prohibits alternate access methods, leaving no clear supported recovery workflow even though the browser documentation describes local development servers.

Related reports: #45230 and #46729. This report adds a verified historical successful interaction sequence and a shipped-file comparison, rather than claiming a new regression or requesting removal of safety checks. Please consolidate if appropriate.

### Observed evidence
- On 2026-09-19, historical native task records show successful IAB accessibility reads, screenshots, and clicks through a loopback HTTP URL. Observed interactions included pause, a resource-changing control, and reset. This was actual agent interaction, not only manual user preview.
- After project migration, the entry became file:///.../index.html (private directory redacted). Browser Use rejected the file URL. A later attempt to select the existing file-backed tab was also blocked.
- The user can manually preview the project, but that does not establish agent access.
- Exact errors include: "Browser Use rejected this action due to browser security policy. Reason: The browser URL policy blocks this action." and "Blocked browser navigation by Browser Use URL policy: file:///.../index.html".
- The accompanying rejection explicitly prohibits workarounds and alternate browser surfaces. We did not bypass it or switch the denied content to another endpoint.

### Read-only diagnostic findings
The inspected browser-service.mjs contains a URL check accepting about:blank and URLs whose parsed protocol is http: or https:, rejecting file: before page interaction.
The runtime default service file and the corresponding file in the installed Windows application bundle have identical SHA-256:
FA354758746C6D4569A3D63474246BA64DCFB9A3F2572927218AFA281CB281C3
The separately configured cached browser-service copy has the same protocol predicate. This comparison supports that the inspected restriction exists in the shipped file; it does not establish every historical process's effective configuration or prove the entire installation is unmodified.

We have not established that any previous version supported direct file URL automation. Historical HTTP success is not evidence of historical file URL success. We have not established an update regression or a shared cause with earlier network/proxy initialization failures.

### Reproduction sequence from observed records
1. Open a local HTML prototype through a loopback development URL: agent interaction succeeded in the historical run.
2. Later open the migrated prototype using a direct file URL.
3. Ask Browser Use to inspect/interact with that page: URL-policy refusal.
4. Manual preview remains possible, while automated visual validation is blocked.
A standalone minimal reproducer has not been executed after the refusal; the sequence above describes recorded observations, not a fresh experiment.

### Expected behavior / clarification requested
1. Is direct file URL automation intentionally unsupported in this Windows version? If so, please document manual preview versus agent-control support separately.
2. Please expose an actionable diagnostic distinguishing unsupported schemes from user-denied origins and managed policy restrictions.
3. What is the supported way to resume normal local-development browser validation after this explicit refusal? In particular, how can a user obtain an approved development-server workflow without asking the agent to circumvent the earlier refusal?
4. If this is a defect, please identify a fixed version or supported recovery action. We are not requesting a global policy relaxation or a patch that removes safety checks.

### Documentation and impact
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser describes local development-server interaction and manual file-backed previews.
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference documents HTTP/HTTPS origin policies; it does not provide a file-scheme approval path.
The practical impact is an incomplete automated visual/interaction acceptance loop, with users otherwise pushed toward manual screenshots and testing. Local code checks are not a substitute for that acceptance.

Only this sanitized summary is published. No project source, private directory paths, raw transcripts, credentials, screenshots, or session identifiers are attached. No browser policy or installed application files were modified for this report.

items.body:
### Environment

- Codex Desktop / ChatGPT macOS app: `26.915.31945` (build `9922`)
- Bundled Codex runtime observed: `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`
- Platform: macOS / Apple Silicon

### What I am trying to establish

I need a supported task/project-local permission route where one exact project root is writable and all other filesystem paths remain read-only.

Concretely, the desired contract is:

- exact project root `T`: write
- all outside paths: read-only
- no broad `/private/tmp` write
- no `TMPDIR` write
- no extra visualization/cache write outside `T`
- supported effective-policy readback
- supported rollback/unload procedure

This is for a bounded disposable containment test, not for bypassing Codex security controls.

### What I observed

A project-local test configuration attempted to use a restricted `workspace-write` setup with:

- `approval_policy = "never"`
- `approvals_reviewer = "user"`
- `exclude_slash_tmp = true`
- `exclude_tmpdir_env_var = true`
- no extra writable roots

The actual Desktop turn context did **not** become T-only. The effective policy reported:

- `approval_policy = on-request`
- reviewer = `auto_review`
- `exclude_slash_tmp = false`
- `exclude_tmpdir_env_var = false`
- writable roots including the project root plus the Desktop visualization directory

No live write/negative containment probes were run after this mismatch.

This does **not** prove that project-local named profiles are unsupported. I could not establish from supported product surfaces whether the project-local values were never loaded, loaded and overridden, or bypassed by a different Desktop permission selector.

### Build-specific implementation evidence

Read-only inspection of the installed app bundle shows that Desktop computes an additional visualization path for the turn.

For legacy `workspaceWrite` handling, that path is added to writable roots.

For a named permissions profile, the code path is different: the profile id is passed separately and the visualization path can be present as a runtime/environment root. From this alone I cannot conclude whether runtime-root membership itself grants write access, or whether the named profile's filesystem rules still control access.

That distinction is the blocker.

### Questions for maintainers

For **Desktop 26.915.31945 / runtime 0.155.0-alpha.9.2**:

1. What is the **supported Desktop selector** for activating a project-local named permission profile for one task/thread?
2. What is the **supported effective-policy readback** that shows:
   - the active named profile,
   - effective filesystem rules,
   - runtime roots,
   - approval policy/reviewer,
   - and the final writable paths?
3. Does the Desktop-injected visualization runtime root gain **write access independently of the selected named profile**, or only when that profile's filesystem rules grant write to it?
4. Is there a supported way for a named profile to express:
   - absolute project root = write,
   - all other paths = read-only,
   - no `:workspace_roots` write,
   - no `:slash_tmp` / `:tmpdir` write?
5. What is the supported **rollback/unload** procedure to prove that the task no longer uses the test profile after the experiment?

If this exact route is unsupported in this Desktop build, a confirmation of that boundary would also resolve the question.

### Why this matters

Without a supported selector + readback contract, it is difficult to distinguish:

- a valid exact-path named profile,
- a project config that was not loaded,
- a Desktop override,
- and a runtime-injected root that may or may not itself be writable.

That makes it unsafe to claim task-scoped filesystem containment from UI labels or config intent alone.

### Notes

- No private repository names, credentials, host identifiers, or user-specific paths are included here.
- No private IPC/RPC was used.
- No CLI substitution was used.
- No global security settings were changed for this report.

Relevant docs:
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/permissions
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/permission-modes

items.body:
## Summary

On 2026-09-22, Codex Desktop on Windows lost its authentication state and I signed in again.

Immediately afterward, my local Codex history disappeared. Investigation shows this was not only a sidebar/indexing issue: the existing `%USERPROFILE%\.codex` directory appears to have been selectively reinitialized in place.

The directory itself survived and still contained older plugin/cache data, but durable local state was recreated around 18:51 local time:

- `installation_id` was regenerated
- `state_5.sqlite` was recreated and contains `threads = 0`
- `goals_1.sqlite`, `queue_1.sqlite`, and `memories_1.sqlite` were recreated
- `.sandbox/setup_marker.json` was newly created as part of provisioning
- `sessions/` no longer exists
- local user-created skills under `.codex/skills/` disappeared
- previous local Codex worktree registrations disappeared

At the same time, account-backed data such as remote plugins was downloaded again after sign-in.

This resulted in permanent loss of local-only Codex conversation history and local skills.

## Environment

- OS: Windows x64
- Product: Codex Desktop
- Auth mode: ChatGPT account
- `CODEX_HOME`: `%USERPROFILE%\.codex`
- Local timezone: UTC+08:00
- Exact Desktop build: not captured during the incident

## Timeline

All times below are local time.

### Before the incident

Earlier on the same day, the existing `.codex` home was confirmed to contain:

- local Codex worktrees
- historical thread/session state
- local user-created skills
- existing plugins and configuration

### 18:51

Filesystem timestamps and application logs show a new initialization sequence:

- ~18:51:21 — new `installation_id`
- ~18:51:21 — `state_5.sqlite`, goals/queue/memories state recreated
- 18:51:21 — auth manager reload:
  `Reloading auth -> Reloaded auth, changed: false`
- 18:51:21 — `project/list`
- 18:51:21 — `config/batchWrite`
- 18:51:28 — multiple `plugin/install` / `plugin/installed`
- 18:51:55 — new `.sandbox/setup_marker.json`
- 18:51:59 — remote plugin catalog fetch
- 18:52:04 — remote installed plugin bundle sync completed

After this sequence, the Desktop UI contained no historical local Codex conversations.

## Evidence that this was a selective in-place reset

The entire `.codex` directory was not deleted and recreated.

Older data remained in place:

- `plugins/` retained ~2026-09-19 timestamps
- `.tmp/` retained ~2026-09-18/19 timestamps
- existing plugin cache content survived

But core local state was newly created at ~18:51.

This makes a selective reset/reinitialization much more consistent with the observed filesystem state than whole-directory deletion.

Additional evidence:

- current `state_5.sqlite` integrity check: OK
- current `threads` row count: `0`
- `sessions/` directory: absent
- Windows Recycle Bin contains no Codex deletion event in the incident window
- no VSS snapshot was available
- the NTFS USN journal retained records only from 18:51:33 onward, while the relevant filesystem changes occurred around 18:51:16–18:51:21, so the decisive delete/rename records had already rolled out
- `.codex-global-state.json` contains:
  - `local-projects: {}`
  - migration state equivalent to:
    - `projectsMigrated: true`
    - `threadAssignmentsMigrated: false`

I cannot identify the exact destructive filesystem operation retroactively, so I am not claiming which component performed it.

## Data loss

An older independent rescue snapshot from 2026-08-29 contains:

- 998 historical Codex thread metadata rows
- titles
- first user messages
- previews
- timestamps
- cwd/project/model metadata

However, all referenced historical rollout JSONL files are missing.

For the period from 2026-08-29 through 2026-09-22, no recoverable local Codex thread/session data was found anywhere on the machine after exhaustive search.

Local user-created skills were also lost during the reinitialization.

Account-backed plugins were re-downloaded successfully after sign-in, which highlights the difference between cloud-backed state and local-only state.

## WAL / recovery investigation

The post-incident SQLite WAL files were preserved and examined offline.

Page-level WAL carving showed that the WAL belongs entirely to the newly created post-18:51 database generation. It contains schema pages but no historical `threads` rows.

So this is not merely a UI indexing failure with recoverable old rows hidden in the current database.

## Expected behavior

Re-authentication should never destroy or recreate durable local user data.

At minimum, the following should survive login/auth changes and provisioning:

- `sessions/`
- `archived_sessions/`
- rollout JSONL transcripts
- `state_5.sqlite` historical thread records
- local user-created skills
- local worktree/session metadata

If a migration or provisioning path requires rebuilding local state, the app should first create a timestamped backup and should never classify local transcripts or user skills as regenerable cache data.

## Actual behavior

A sign-in/reinitialization sequence left the existing CODEX_HOME partially intact while recreating its durable state.

Cloud-backed content was rehydrated afterward, but local-only Codex history and skills were not recoverable.

## Related issues

This appears related to the same Windows local-state/data-loss family as:

- #37419 — selective CODEX_HOME runtime directory deletion
- #41048 — hundreds of local rollout JSONL transcripts deleted
- #41874 — incomplete project/thread-assignment migration
- #27734 — local transcript data loss after Desktop update

The important difference in this case is that the local state database itself was also recreated with zero threads, and local user skills disappeared, while older plugin/cache content in the same CODEX_HOME survived.

## Requested action

Please investigate the authentication / provisioning / migration paths that can selectively reset CODEX_HOME.

In particular:

1. Treat local transcripts, thread state, user skills, and local worktree metadata as durable user data.
2. Never delete or recreate them as part of login, logout, provisioning, sandbox setup, or migration without explicit user confirmation.
3. Before any CODEX_HOME reset/migration, create a timestamped backup of durable user state.
4. Log every destructive operation inside CODEX_HOME with the calling component, reason, and affected paths.
5. If thread metadata and rollout files disagree, surface the corruption instead of silently presenting an empty history.
6. Provide a first-party backup/reindex/recovery mechanism for local Codex history.
7. Please clarify whether any OpenAI-side state can recover Codex Desktop local transcripts after this class of loss.

I can provide sanitized filesystem timelines, SQLite schema/row counts, application log excerpts, and recovery reports if useful. I will not upload authentication tokens or `auth.json`.

items.body:
## Feature Request: `image_gen` should support a configurable completion path for headless/bot deployments

### Problem

When running Codex via ACP in a headless deployment (Slack/Discord bot on a server), the `image_gen` system skill generates an image and renders it inline (base64). The skill then marks the task as complete.

However, ACP only streams text — inline images are silently dropped. The user sees "image generated" with no image attached. The agent believes it succeeded; the user received nothing.

### Current behavior

```
image_gen → base64 inline render → task complete ✓
                    ↓
              ACP (text only) → inline image silently dropped
                    ↓
              User sees: "已產生圖片" (no image)
```

### Expected behavior

In headless deployments (no screen), `image_gen` should support an alternative completion path — for example, saving the file to a configurable directory and NOT treating inline render as task completion, so the agent (or the platform) can handle the upload step.

```
image_gen → save to file → agent/platform uploads to chat → task complete ✓
```

### Evidence: steering cannot override this

We tested five approaches to make the agent upload proactively via steering/instructions — all passive approaches failed because `image_gen`'s built-in completion behavior overrides any steering rules:

| # | Approach | Result |
|---|----------|--------|
| 1 | CRITICAL warning in steering: "inline images are not forwarded" | ❌ Overridden by system skill |
| 2 | Full curl upload template in steering | ❌ Overridden |
| 3 | Definition of Done rewrite: "upload to Slack = complete" | ❌ Overridden |
| 4 | `~/.codex/instructions.md` with short DoD rule | ❌ Overridden |
| 5 | User explicitly says "generate image AND upload to this thread" | ✅ Works every time |

Only explicit user instruction (experiment 5) works — passive steering cannot change the skill's completion behavior.

### Environment

- codex-acp: `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` (latest)
- Platform: Slack (Socket Mode) via [OpenAB](https://github.com/openabdev/openab)
- Cluster: GKE Autopilot (headless, no display)

### Suggested solution

A configuration option (e.g., in `~/.codex/config.toml` or a session-level setting) that controls `image_gen`'s completion behavior:

```toml
# Example: don't treat inline render as task completion in headless mode
[skills.image_gen]
completion = "file"  # "inline" (default) | "file" (save and let agent/platform handle delivery)
output_dir = "~/.codex/generated_images/"
```

Or alternatively, respect `CODEX_HEADLESS=true` / `sandbox_mode` to automatically adjust skill completion behavior when running without a display.

### Current workaround

We run a file-watcher CronJob sidecar that polls `~/.codex/generated_images/` every minute, reverse-lookups the originating chat thread, and uploads via the platform API. This works but adds operational complexity that a configurable skill completion path would eliminate.

### References

- [OpenAB issue #1541](https://github.com/openabdev/openab/issues/1541) — investigation trail with 5 experiments
- [OpenAB PR #1542](https://github.com/openabdev/openab/pull/1542) — attempted platform-level fix (reviewer correctly identified root cause belongs in agent/skill layer)
- [OpenAB docs/sendimages.md](https://github.com/openabdev/openab/blob/main/docs/sendimages.md) — community documentation for agent-side image delivery
